**How the 380 commits break down:** ~150 dependency bumps, ~90 tests, ~80 refactors, ~30 chore/CI, ~15 docs. That leaves 37 commits that touch behavior, and those collapse into the 15 lines above — most of the fixes are the same fix landed separately in four or five modules (null cursor in `api`/`db`/`queue`/`webhooks`, empty allowlist in `store`/`db`/`jobs`, duplicate header in `core`/`billing`/`http`), so I merged them rather than listing each.

**Three things to check before you publish:**

1. **The history stops on 2026-06-17.** You're cutting on the 29th of August — that's ten weeks unaccounted for. Either the branch genuinely froze in June or this export is stale. If it's stale, everything above is a partial release note.

2. **The two removals I put under Breaking were labelled otherwise by their authors.** `refactor(api): drop the unused v1 export route` and the eight `stop re-exporting the internal error types` commits are all typed as refactors, meaning the team considered that surface private. If it really was private, demote both to a footnote. If anything outside this repo imported it, "unused" was wrong and Breaking is right. Worth one grep across your consumers — it's the difference between a minor and a major bump.

3. **Two fixes I couldn't characterize from the log alone:**
   - `handle an empty allowlist` — I wrote "no longer errors," but the commit could equally mean an empty allowlist previously fell open and now denies everything. That's a security-relevant distinction and you should read the diff before shipping the sentence.
   - `use the right units in the latency histogram` — I noted that recorded values shift, since anyone alerting on those metrics will see thresholds move. Confirm the direction.

**What I deliberately left out:** the 16 dependency bumps are all patch or minor with no visible surface (`pg`, `undici`, `fastify`, `pino`, `knex`, `ioredis` on the runtime side; the rest dev-only) — nothing there for an installer to notice. And the ten `perf` commits: your template has three headings and no performance section, and none of the commits carry a measurement, so a "faster!" line would be an unbacked claim. `perf(api): reuse the parsed schema between requests` is the only one plausibly measurable at the request level — if you have a benchmark for it, that one could justify a line of its own.
